body.heading: Your past self has receipts
paragraphs: In a difficult patch, the mind argues that you cannot cope. But the factual record disagrees: you have coped with every hard day so far, including ones you were sure would undo you. The problem is that in the middle of a new hard thing, the record is hard to recall.
So keep the evidence where your future self can find it. This is not sentimentality; it is logistics. Courage is easier with documents.

body.heading: Build a small evidence file
paragraphs: Start a note — paper or phone — called something like “Proof.” Add entries as they happen: the exam survived, the difficult conversation handled, the month that felt impossible in week one and ordinary by week four. One or two lines each is plenty.

Include the how, not just the what. “I got through the move by asking two friends for help and sleeping properly” teaches your future self a method, not just a fact. Methods are what hard days actually need.

body.heading: Read it like instructions
paragraphs: When a new difficulty arrives, read the file slowly. Notice the pattern in your own history: the fear at the start is always larger than the thing turns out to be, and you have specific moves that help you in particular.
Add to the file afterwards, too — including this difficulty, once it has passed. Your evidence file compounds like interest, and one day someone you love may need to borrow the idea from you.

takeaway: Keep the receipts of your own coping, and read them when the mind argues otherwise.
